title: Mag-Lev Spine Corridor Infrastructure: The Arterial Transit Network of GLMZ
body:
The Spine Corridors are the load-bearing skeleton of GLMZ's transit architecture — four elevated mag-lev trunk lines running roughly north-south and east-west through the megacity's core, intersecting at Confluence Hub in the mid-tier district of Portsmith. Built between 2141 and 2159 under successive infrastructure compacts between the city's dominant corporate sovereigns, the Spine system carries an estimated 4.2 million passenger-trips per day, making it the single most-used transit infrastructure in the Great Lakes basin. The lines are not publicly owned in any meaningful sense: each corridor segment was constructed and is operated by a designated infrastructure concessionaire — Velorant Systems holds the North-South Axis, while Caldor Transit Consortium operates the East-West Crossline under a rolling 30-year franchise renewed in 2171.

Access to Spine Corridor stations is tiered by citizenship grade in ways that are architecturally enforced rather than merely procedural. Tier-One and Tier-Two citizens enter through dedicated biometric gates at street level, passing through climate-conditioned concourses with seating, commercial vendors, and neural-uplink rest zones. Tier-Three citizens access the same physical trains via separate lower-concourse entrances, typically at sub-street level, with longer average wait times engineered into the gate sequencing. Tier-Four and provisional-status residents are nominally permitted on the system but face dynamic pricing that renders regular use economically prohibitive — a 12-stop cross-city trip priced at 0.4 CredUnits for Tier-One passengers costs 2.1 CredUnits at Tier-Four rates during peak hours. The pricing algorithm is proprietary to Velorant and has never been audited by any civic authority.

The trains themselves are impressive engineering artifacts: six-car articulated sets running on embedded magnetic track at operational speeds between 140 and 210 kilometers per hour within the elevated corridors, slowing through dense station zones. Interiors are zoned by car class — Standard, Business, and Executive cars on every train, with Executive cars accessible only to Tier-One passengers or holders of Velorant Premium subscriptions. Standard cars carry the overwhelming majority of daily riders: standing loads averaging 180 percent of design capacity during the 0700-0900 and 1700-1930 rush windows. The ventilation systems in Standard cars have been a chronic maintenance deficit item since 2168; worker advocacy groups document respiratory complaints at three times the Executive car rate.

The four Spine lines converge at Confluence Hub, a transit node of genuine architectural ambition that has become one of the megacity's most surveilled single locations. Approximately 800,000 people pass through Confluence daily. The Hub's upper levels house corporate shuttle connections, executive lounges operated by Harmon Logistics, and a permanent Meridian Security Authority checkpoint station. Lower levels transition into the mid-tier commercial district. The junction between upper and lower levels — colloquially called the Seam — is where the visible economic stratification of the Spine system becomes most legible to daily riders, and where transit-related tension incidents are most frequently logged by MSA patrol units.
